Volume 13 · Chapter 02

Consumer and producer duality

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v13-c01

By the endDerive duality identities and characterize economically admissible demand and cost functions.

Volume 13 · Chapter 2

Consumer and producer duality

A demand equation can balance the budget, respond negatively to its own price and still be incompatible with smooth utility maximization. A profit function can describe every positive price perfectly while concealing a missing production opportunity. Duality gives useful identities because it links optimizations over the same feasible objects. Its hypotheses determine what those identities reveal.

Capability. Prove consumer expenditure and demand identities, qualified price envelopes and Roy’s identity; derive the Slutsky restrictions; construct preferences for a specified homothetic expenditure class; and prove producer envelopes and exactly what profit values reconstruct. Six original worked cases and twelve solved exercises distinguish existence, smoothness and identification.

Prerequisites. Preference representation and choice theory supplies ordinal representation, local nonsatiation and rationalizability. Use the derivative and envelope tools of Volume 2, Chapter 7, convexity and separation from Chapter 9, and compact subsequences from Chapter 10. Elementary consumer theory and Production and costs introduce the economic problems. The general results proved below state their own domains; the shifted domain in case 1 is expressly separate.

1. A budget problem and its expenditure counterpart

Unless another domain is specified, consumption is x∈ℝ+L, with finite L. Prices p≫0 mean every component is strictly positive; income m≥0 and expenditure p·x are in currency units. Utility u(x) is a numerical preference label, not currency. Define

B(p,m)={x≥0:p·x≤m},   v(p,m)=maxx∈B(p,m)u(x),
D(p,m)=argmaxx∈B(p,m)u(x),
A(ū)={x≥0:u(x)≥ū},   e(p,ū)=minx∈A(ū)p·x,
H(p,ū)=argminx∈A(ū)p·x.

D is the Marshallian demand correspondence; H is the Hicksian, or compensated, demand correspondence. A correspondence may contain more than one bundle. A utility target is attainable when A(ū) is nonempty. For unattainable targets define the infimum expenditure as +∞ and H as empty; no finite dual identity is implied. In this section u is continuous and targets satisfy ū≥u(0).

Existence and no excess utility. B(p,m) is nonempty, closed and bounded, since 0≤xi≤m/pi. A continuous function therefore attains its maximum. For expenditure, select one feasible witness z∈A(ū). Any cheaper competitor lies in the compact set {x≥0:p·x≤p·z}; its intersection with the closed A(ū) is nonempty and compact. Minimization there attains the global minimum. Strictly positive prices, rather than just nonnegative prices, supply this bound.

Every expenditure minimizer h satisfies u(h)=ū. Otherwise u(h)>ū≥u(0), so h≠0. Continuity along t↦u(th), 0≤t≤1, gives a t<1 with u(th)=ū. The cheaper feasible th contradicts minimality. This radial argument does not require monotonicity or convex preferences. It is also why a target below u(0) needs a different statement: zero then costs nothing while delivering strictly more than the target.

Exact dual identities. Add local nonsatiation: in every relative neighborhood of every x≥0 there is a bundle with strictly higher utility. Any maximizer spends its budget. If p·x<m, a sufficiently small neighborhood stays affordable, and local nonsatiation contradicts maximality. More generally, no bundle attaining v(p,m) can cost less than m, by the same argument. Since every demanded bundle attains v and spends m,

e(p,v(p,m))=m,   H(p,v(p,m))=D(p,m).

For an attainable ū≥u(0), let e=e(p,ū) and h∈H. Then u(h)=ū and h is feasible at income e. If a bundle y in B(p,e) had u(y)>ū, the same radial intermediate-value argument would give t<1 with u(ty)=ū. Here y≠0 and p·ty<p·y≤e, contradicting minimal expenditure. Therefore v(p,e)=ū. Every demand at that income has utility ū and, under local nonsatiation, expenditure e; it belongs to H. Conversely every h belongs to the demand set. Thus

v(p,e(p,ū))=ū,   D(p,e(p,ū))=H(p,ū).

At m=0 the budget contains only zero; at target u(0), the least expenditure is zero. These boundary cases are included. Local nonsatiation is needed for budget exhaustion and the inverse identity starting from income; the no-excess and expenditure-to-utility arguments used continuity and the target restriction. Continuity alone, for example a constant utility, would not give e(p,v(p,m))=m at positive income.

2. Price changes, kinks and Roy’s denominator

Fix an attainable target. Since the feasible set A(ū) does not change with prices, expenditure is an infimum of linear functions. For 0≤t≤1 and positive p,q, every feasible x has [tp+(1−t)q]·x≥t e(p,ū)+(1−t)e(q,ū); minimize to prove concavity. Direct minimization gives e(tp,ū)=t e(p,ū) for t>0. Nonnegative quantities make e weakly increasing in every price.

Supporting quantities. For any h∈H(p,ū), its feasibility at another price gives

e(q,ū)≤q·h=e(p,ū)+(q−p)·h.

This is the supporting supergradient inequality for a concave function. The sign points downward from the supporting plane. No differentiability or unique minimizer was used.

Why the envelope is a derivative when demand is unique. Near p≫0, prices have a common positive lower bound. A fixed feasible witness bounds nearby optimal expenditures, and hence every nearby Hicksian optimizer. If pn→p and hn is optimal at pn, take a convergent subsequence. Closed feasibility preserves its limit h*. Comparing each hn with a fixed optimizer h at p yields limsup pn·hn≤p·h=e(p,ū), whereas feasible h* has p·h*≥e(p,ū). Thus every such limit is optimal at p. If H(p,ū)={h}, all nearby optimizers converge to h: a subsequence bounded away from h would have a contradictory convergent further subsequence.

For small vector δ and an optimizer hδ at p+δ, the two optimality comparisons give

δ·hδ ≤ e(p+δ,ū)−e(p,ū) ≤ δ·h.

The gap is bounded in magnitude by ‖δ‖‖hδ−h‖=o(‖δ‖). Therefore e is differentiable at p and ∇pe=h: Shephard’s identity. This proof supplies the optimizer control that a formal differentiation of an optimum might omit.

Without uniqueness, H(p,ū) is still compact. For a fixed direction d and t↓0, choose hd∈H minimizing d·h. The upper comparison uses hd, while all subsequential limits of the nearby optimizers are in H. The lower comparison therefore has liminf at least minHd·h. Together they prove the one-sided directional formula

e′(p,ū;d)=limt↓0[e(p+td,ū)−e(p,ū)]/t=minh∈H(p,ū)d·h.

Roy’s identity. Suppose v is differentiable on an open neighborhood of an interior point p≫0,m>0, and take any x∈D(p,m). Budget exhaustion gives p·x=m. Along (p+td,m+t d·x), that same x remains affordable for both signs of small t. Consequently v(p+td,m+t d·x)≥v(p,m), with equality at t=0, so the derivative there is zero. Every direction d gives d·(vp+vmx)=0. Thus vp=−vmx. Only with the additional condition vm>0 may we divide:

xi(p,m)=−vpi(p,m)/vm(p,m).

Utility per price unit divided by utility per currency unit has quantity units. Differentiability and positive vm also imply all demanded bundles coincide. Ordinal preference monotonicity alone does not force a particular numerical utility representation to have a positive income derivative.

Worked case 1: subsistence and two money measures

Here the consumption domain is explicitly X=γ+ℝ+2, with γ=(1,2), and u(x)=√[(x₁−1)(x₂−2)]. This is a separate shifted-domain calculation, not an application of a theorem whose domain contains zero. Prices are positive and m≥p·γ. Write z=x−γ and surplus income M=m−p·γ. For target ū≥0, z₁z₂≥ū² and the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality gives p₁z₁+p₂z₂≥2√(p₁p₂z₁z₂)≥2ū√(p₁p₂). Equality requires p₁z₁=p₂z₂ and z₁z₂=ū². Positive prices make the zero-target minimizer z=0 unique as well. Hence

e(p,ū)=p·γ+2ū√(p₁p₂),
h(p,ū)=γ+ū(√(p₂/p₁),√(p₁/p₂)).

For a fixed budget, (p₁z₁+p₂z₂)²≥4p₁p₂z₁z₂ bounds utility by M/[2√(p₁p₂)]. Equal expenditure on the two surplus quantities attains this bound. Thus the unique demand is x=γ+M(1/(2p₁),1/(2p₂)), including M=0. At p=(4,1) and m=14, the demand and utility are ((2,6),2).

Differentiate at fixed m: ∂xi/∂pj=−γj/(2pi)−1{i=j}M/(2pi²), while xm=(1/(2p₁),1/(2p₂)). Numerically,

Dpx=((−3/8,−1/4),(−1/2,−5)),   xm=(1/8,1/2).

The compensated matrix Dpx+xmx′ is ((−1/8,1/2),(1/2,−2)). Its quadratic form at direction d is −(d₁−4d₂)²/8≤0, and it annihilates p=(4,1). The uncompensated cross derivatives −1/4 and −1/2 differ; the compensated cross derivatives both equal 1/2.

Now increase prices to p′=(9,1), holding m=14. Subsistence costs 11, leaving surplus 3; new demand and utility are ((7/6,7/2),1/2). Define positive welfare losses for this adverse change: compensating variation loss CV=e(p′,uold)−m is the income addition at new prices needed to restore old utility; equivalent variation loss EV=m−e(p,unew) is the income removal at old prices that reproduces new utility. Here e(p′,2)=23 and e(p,1/2)=8, so (9,6) is (CV,EV). These signs are conventions stated for losses; neither number is a utility difference.

Worked case 2: a price kink and an ordinally flat derivative

First take u(x)=x₁+2x₂, target 6, and positive prices. Each unit of the utility target can be purchased for p₁ through good 1 or p₂/2 through good 2. Expenditure is 6 min(p₁,p₂/2). At prices (2,4), it equals 12, and every bundle in H={x≥0:x₁+2x₂=6} minimizes. The segment endpoints are ((6,0),(0,3)). Its support formula is e′(p,6;d)=min(6d₁,3d₂). With p₂ fixed, the derivative with respect to p₁ is 6 approaching from below and 0 from above, the pair (6,0). A single Hicksian selection cannot be an ordinary gradient at this kink, though every minimizer supplies a valid concave supporting plane.

Separately take u(x)=(x₁+x₂−3)³. Cubing is strictly increasing, so this represents exactly the same preference as total goods x₁+x₂. On the open region p₁<p₂, the unique demand is (m/p₁,0), and v=(m/p₁−3)³. At (p₁,p₂,m)=(1,2,3), the common derivative factor 3(m/p₁−3)² vanishes. Thus (vp₁,vp₂,vm)=(0,0,0), although the unique demand is (3,0). Dividing 0 by 0 is not an envelope identity.

Use the ordinally equivalent index w=x₁+x₂ instead. Its indirect value m/p₁ has derivatives (−m/p₁²,0,1/p₁), numerically (−3,0,1), and valid Roy division recovers (3,0). The first example loses a gradient because optimizers vary across a price tie; the second has unique demand but a representation with a zero derivative denominator.

The inspected consumer-theory scope in Wolitzky’s MIT lectures provides further reading on these dual methods. The compactness, target and derivative conditions used here are part of the stated proofs, not assumptions supplied by a citation alone.

3. Compensated symmetry is more than a downward slope

Suppose we are in a neighborhood with unique demands, a continuously differentiable Marshallian function x(p,m), a continuously differentiable Hicksian function h(p,ū), and differentiable expenditure satisfying h=∇pe. Fix a feasible utility target with positive expenditure and maintain the dual identity h(p,ū)=x(p,e(p,ū)). Define row i, column j by Sij=∂hi/∂pj. The chain rule gives

S=Dpx+xmx′,   Sij=∂xi/∂pj+(∂xi/∂m)xj.

When pj increases, compensation at the margin is xj currency units per unit of that price increase. This explains the product and its sign. Since C¹ h makes e twice continuously differentiable, equality of mixed partials gives S=S′. Price concavity gives d′Sd≤0 for every d: restrict e to the line p+td and differentiate twice. Hicksian homogeneity h(tp,ū)=h(p,ū) implies Sp=0 by differentiation at t=1. Symmetry then gives p′S=0. These are compensated restrictions, not general sign restrictions on every Marshallian cross derivative.

The result is necessary within this regular smooth expenditure model. We have not proved that a field satisfying a few pointwise restrictions can be integrated globally into a utility representation on an arbitrary domain. The next two cases show, respectively, a failure of the necessary restrictions and a constructive sufficient result for a clearly specified class.

Worked case 3: a balanced demand field that cannot be a smooth compensated gradient

For three goods use cyclic indices and let ε=1/12. On the open, scale-invariant domain p≫0 with maxilog pi−minilog pi<1 and m>0, set

si(p)=1/3+ε[log pi+1−log pi+2],   xi(p,m)=m si(p)/pi.

The shares lie strictly between 1/4 and 5/12. Their log differences cancel in the sum, so Σsi=1 and p·x=m. Scaling all prices leaves every share unchanged; scaling prices and income together leaves x unchanged. Each share omits its own price, giving ∂xi/∂pi=−m si/pi²<0. Positivity is asserted only on this domain, not at every positive price ratio.

Let A have rows (0,1,−1),(−1,0,1),(1,−1,0). Then ∂si/∂pj=ε Aij/pj, and direct differentiation yields Sij=m[ε Aij+sisj−1{i=j}si]/(pipj). At p=(1,1,1) and m=3, demand is (1,1,1) and

S=((−2/3,7/12,1/12),(1/12,−2/3,7/12),(7/12,1/12,−2/3)).

Write P=I−11′/3. It is a symmetric projection: P²=P. The matrix is S=−P+A/4. Its rows and columns sum to zero, and the skew symmetry A′=−A gives z′Az=0. Therefore z′Sz=−z′Pz=−‖Pz‖²≤0 for every z. Nevertheless S₁₂=7/12 differs from S₂₁=1/12. Negative quadratic forms do not remove a skew component. This smooth field fails the necessary symmetry condition for the regular expenditure rationalization just proved, despite satisfying the budget, homogeneity and own-price checks. The conclusion does not invoke a generic theorem about every possible nonsmooth rationalization.

4. A constructive homothetic integrability theorem

Here is a sufficient construction with a full domain and an explicit candidate preference. Let c:ℝ++L→(0,∞) be C¹, concave, homogeneous of degree one, with ∇c(p)≥0. Define for x≥0

U(x)=infq≫0 q·x/c(q).

Each ratio is a nonnegative linear function of x. Choosing one fixed q bounds the infimum above by a finite value, so U is finite and nonnegative. An infimum of linear functions is concave by the same direct inequality used for expenditure; positive coefficients make U weakly monotone. For t≥0, U(tx)=tU(x), including U(0)=0. Its upper contour {U≥ū} is the intersection of the closed half-spaces q·x≥ū c(q). No general boundary-continuity theorem is being presumed.

Constructive dual proof. Differentiating c(tp)=t c(p) at t=1 gives Euler’s identity p·∇c(p)=c(p). Concavity supplies c(q)≤c(p)+∇c(p)·(q−p)=q·∇c(p). For any target ū≥0, the nonnegative witness h=ū∇c(p) consequently has q·h/c(q)≥ū at every q, with equality at q=p. Thus U(h)=ū and p·h=ū c(p). Every bundle with U(x)≥ū satisfies the price-p inequality p·x≥ū c(p). Therefore

e(p,ū)=ū c(p),   ū∇c(p)∈H(p,ū).

Similarly, any affordable x has U(x)≤p·x/c(p)≤m/c(p), while x*=m∇c(p)/c(p) is affordable and attains that value. Hence v(p,m)=m/c(p), with x* a constructed Marshallian demand. The explicit witnesses establish attainment even though the infimum defining U ranges over a noncompact price domain. This is a constructive sufficient theorem for this homothetic class. It is not a general global Marshallian-integrability theorem, and we do not infer arbitrary demand uniqueness without a separate argument.

Worked case 4: reconstruct a direct index and integrate compensation

Choose c(p)=2√(p₁p₂)+p₃ on all p≫0. It is positive and degree one, with gradient (√(p₂/p₁),√(p₁/p₂),1). For a price direction d its Hessian quadratic form is −√(p₁p₂)(d₁/p₁−d₂/p₂)²/2≤0. Along any price segment this proves concavity. The constructive theorem applies.

Its direct index is U(x)=min(√(x₁x₂),x₃). To verify the infimum formula, the ratio q·x/[2√(q₁q₂)+q₃] is a weighted average of (q₁x₁+q₂x₂)/(2√(q₁q₂)) and x₃. The first term is at least √(x₁x₂), by AM–GM, so every ratio is at least their minimum. Sending q₃ to infinity gives a limiting ratio x₃. If x₁,x₂>0, choose q₁/q₂=x₂/x₁ and let q₃↓0 to obtain √(x₁x₂). If one of x₁,x₂ is zero, make the price on that zero quantity large relative to the other, keeping q₃ bounded, to obtain limit zero; if both are zero let q₃↓0. These positive-price sequences prove equality at every nonnegative x.

Directly, U(x)≥ū requires x₁x₂≥ū² and x₃≥ū. AM–GM and positive p₃ give minimum expenditure ū[2√(p₁p₂)+p₃] at the unique bundle (ū√(p₂/p₁),ū√(p₁/p₂),ū), with the zero-target case uniquely x=0. At p=(1,4,2) and ū=3, this gives (c,h,e)=(6,(6,3/2,3),18). Income m=18 therefore attains utility 3.

Change prices to p′=(4,1,2). The compensated bundle becomes (3/2,6,3), but expenditure remains 18. Integrate h·dp with utility fixed. Along the path changing p₁ first, expenditure rises from 18 to 30 and then returns to 18; along the path changing p₂ first it falls to 12 and then returns to 18. The segment increments are ((12,−12),(−6,6)). For example, ∫₁⁴3√(4/p₁) dp₁=12. Both totals are zero because this field is the gradient of a global expenditure potential.

Integrating a gradient alone leaves an additive constant, but expenditure homogeneity does not. Replacing c by c+1 preserves ∇c yet gives c(tp)+1=t c(p)+1, different from t[c(p)+1] when t≠1. Also p·∇c=c, not c+1. At positive target ū the putative gradient bundle costs ūc(p), contradicting the proposed value ū[c(p)+1]. Economic restrictions eliminate this mathematical integration ambiguity.

5. Cost is concave in input prices; profit is convex in all prices

A production vector y lists net outputs: positive coordinates are delivered goods and negative coordinates are used inputs. For a price-independent feasible set Y, profit is π(p)=supy∈Yp·y. A firm paying input prices w and receiving output price r uses p=(w,r) and y=(−z,q). Profit is therefore rq−w·z. Finite profit and attained supply are assumptions to verify; even the closed set {y≥0} has infinite profit at a positive scalar price.

Value and supply restrictions. Where finite, π is convex because each p·y is linear and a supremum satisfies π(tp+(1−t)q)≤tπ(p)+(1−t)π(q). It is degree one by scaling the same supremum. If y supplies optimally at p and z at q, the inequalities p·y≥p·z and q·z≥q·y imply (p−q)·(y−z)≥0. This is the joint monotonicity restriction, not a claim that every component of supply rises with every price.

For an envelope, assume Y is closed, profit is finite and attained in a neighborhood, chosen optimizers there are uniformly bounded, and supply at p is unique. Limit points of nearby optimizers are feasible by closedness. Comparing values against the optimizer at p shows every limit is optimal there, hence equals it. The same compact-subsequence argument as for expenditure gives convergence. The profit comparisons now give δ·y≤π(p+δ)−π(p)≤δ·yδ, so ∇π(p)=y. These are Hotelling’s net-supply identities. If π is C², convexity implies a symmetric positive-semidefinite Hessian. Differentiating degree-zero ∇π gives (D²π)p=0.

For a target output q, let Z(q) be its feasible input set and C(w,q)=infz∈Z(q)w·z. Holding q fixed, the same input-price argument as for expenditure makes C concave and degree one in w. With a closed feasible input set, attainment, local boundedness and uniqueness, its price gradient is the conditional input vector z≥0. Thus ∂C/∂wi=zi has a nonnegative sign, whereas ∂π/∂wi=−zi for the firm’s optimizing output. This does not say input demand has a positive own-price derivative: the differentiable conditional input Jacobian is the negative-semidefinite cost Hessian.

Curvature in q is a separate matter. If the set of feasible (z,q) is convex, mixing cost-minimizing feasible plans for q₀,q₁ gives a feasible plan for tq₀+(1−t)q₁ at mixed cost. Minimization implies C(w,tq₀+(1−t)q₁)≤tC(w,q₀)+(1−t)C(w,q₁), whenever the relevant finite minima exist. A concave production function gives such a convex feasible hypograph. Price concavity alone says nothing about output convexity; case 6 supplies a counterexample.

Worked case 5: diminishing returns and the full net-supply Hessian

Let output be f(k,l)=(kl)1/4, k,l≥0, with positive input prices w₁,w₂ and target q≥0. Producing at least q requires kl≥q⁴. AM–GM gives w₁k+w₂l≥2√(w₁w₂kl)≥2q²√(w₁w₂), with equality at

k=q²√(w₂/w₁),   l=q²√(w₁/w₂),   C(w,q)=2q²√(w₁w₂).

The equality conditions prove global conditional optimality and uniqueness, including q=0. For fixed q the price Hessian quadratic form is −q²√(w₁w₂)(d₁/w₁−d₂/w₂)²/2≤0. For fixed positive w, Cqq=4√(w₁w₂)>0. The opposite curvatures concern different arguments.

At output price r≥0, write s=√(w₁w₂). Completing the square gives rq−2sq²=r²/(8s)−2s[q−r/(4s)]². The unique maximizing q on q≥0 is r/(4s), including r=0; consequently π(w,r)=r²/(8s). This proves a finite attained optimum by the quadratic penalty, rather than by closedness alone.

At w=(1,4) and r=8, (q,k,l,C,π)=(1,2,1/2,4,4). In the coordinate order (w₁,w₂,r), the profit gradient is (−2,−1/2,1). Its price dot product is 4, verifying Euler’s identity. The full Hessian is

D²π=((3,1/4,−1/2),(1/4,3/16,−1/8),(−1/2,−1/8,1/8)).

For any positive r, let a=dw₁/w₁, b=dw₂/w₂ and ρ=dr/r. Differentiating π=r²w₁−1/2w₂−1/2/8 gives πwᵢwᵢ=3π/(4wᵢ²), πw₁w₂=π/(4w₁w₂), πwᵢr=−π/(wᵢr) and πrr=2π/r². Its quadratic form is

d′D²π d=π{2[ρ−(a+b)/2]²+(a−b)²/4}≥0.

This exact square certificate establishes positive semidefiniteness without approximate eigenvalues. It vanishes on the common-scale direction a=b=ρ, so the Hessian annihilates (w₁,w₂,r). At r=0 use the explicit function and one-sided output-price domain rather than the formula containing dr/r. If the input prices are swapped to (4,1) with r=8, output and profit stay fixed while input quantities exchange: (1,1/2,2,4,4) in the same (q,k,l,C,π) order.

The scoped producer discussion in Condie’s advanced microeconomics notes, section 3.2 provides further method context. Here closedness, finiteness, attainment and local optimizer bounds are separate hypotheses; the specific models establish their own optimality conditions.

6. What observing every profit value can recover

Take a nonempty compact generating set K⊂ℝL. Let Yc=co(K)−ℝ+L: convex mixtures of generators followed by free disposal. Free disposal allows any coordinate to be reduced; with net outputs this includes discarding output or using additional inputs. We will prove

Yc={y:p·y≤maxk∈Kp·k for every p≫0}.

Compact hull and closed disposal set. Every finite convex combination can be reduced to at most L+1 points. If more positive weights remain, the vectors (kj,1) in ℝL+1 are linearly dependent. There are coefficients α, not all zero, with Σαjkj=0 and Σαj=0. Some α are positive. Replace weights λ by λ−tα, where t=minαⱼ>0λj/αj. The represented point and total weight stay fixed, every weight remains nonnegative, and at least one becomes zero. Repeat. Thus co(K) is the continuous image of the compact product KL+1 times a compact simplex, allowing zero weights, and is compact.

If yn=an−bn→y with an∈co(K), bn≥0, a subsequence has an→a in co(K). Then bn→a−y≥0, so y∈Yc. Hence Yc is closed, as well as convex and free-disposal. For any p≥0 its support is maxKp·k: disposal cannot improve the linear objective, and convex mixtures cannot exceed their largest generator value. This proves one inclusion in the displayed reconstruction.

Why strictly positive prices suffice. If z∉Yc, strict separation of a point from a nonempty closed convex set gives a nonzero vector p with p·z>supy∈Ycp·y. No component of p can be negative: reducing that coordinate of a feasible y without bound would make p·y arbitrarily large. Thus p≥0 and δ=p·z−maxKp·k>0. To remove zero price components set pε=p+ε1≫0. Compact K makes M=maxK|1·k| finite, and its support changes by at most εM. Therefore

pε·z−maxKpε·k ≥ δ−ε(|1·z|+M)>0

for sufficiently small ε>0. A strictly positive price still excludes z, proving the reverse inclusion. The argument requires the full set of positive-price inequalities, not finitely many observed prices.

If the actual set is the possibly nonconvex Y₀=K−ℝ+L, both Y₀ and Yc have exactly the same profit maxKp·k at every positive price. The reconstruction gives the closed convex free-disposal hull. It cannot decide whether mixtures absent from Y₀ are actually feasible. Value equality also does not imply that supply correspondences coincide at prices with tied generators.

Worked case 6: entry, capacity and an invisible production gap

There is one input priced at w>0 and one output priced at r>0. Let K={(0,0)}∪{(−4−q²,q):0≤q≤3}, a compact set, and Y₀=K−ℝ+2. The inactive plan is feasible; the active plan incurs a fixed input requirement 4 and has capacity 3. Conditional minimum input is 0 at target q=0, 4+q² for 0<q≤3, and +∞ for q>3. Monetary conditional cost multiplies these amounts by w. In particular C(w,1)=5w>[C(w,0)+C(w,2)]/2=4w, so output convexity fails despite linearity in w.

Write a=r/w. The active objective is w(aq−4−q²). It is strictly concave in q, with stationary quantity a/2, truncated to the capacity 3. Compare its maximum with the inactive profit zero. All branches are:

Profit and complete original supply choices
Price ratioOutput choicesProfit
0<a<40, inactive0
a=40, inactive; or 2, active0
4<a<6a/2r²/(4w)−4w
a≥63; unique also at a=63r−13w

At w=1 and r values (3,4,5,7), profits are (0,0,9/4,8). The output choices in the same order are (0,(0,2),5/2,3). At r=3 the positive stationary candidate has (q,active profit)=(3/2,−7/4), so a first-order condition without the participation comparison would make a loss.

At entry r=4,w=1, the original net supplies are ((0,0),(−8,2)). The one-sided output-price derivatives of profit are (0,2), so Hotelling cannot be read as a single differentiable gradient there. At the capacity boundary r=6,w=1 the interior and capped gradients both equal (−13,3). Profit is differentiable there, but its second derivative with respect to r changes from 1/2 to 0.

Convexification adds every mixture between the two entry plans. Half of each gives (−4,1). This point is absent from Y₀: to provide at least one unit of output an active generator needs at least 5 input units; inactivity cannot provide it, and free disposal cannot create output or reduce input use. Nevertheless every positive-price profit is unchanged by convexification. At the entry tie the hull has the entire connecting supply segment, whereas the original technology has only its two endpoints. A complete profit-value function does not reveal that nonconvex gap.

7. A proof and computation workflow

Declare first which object is fixed: income for Marshallian changes, utility for compensated changes, output for conditional costs, or technology for profit comparisons. Establish finite attainment before differentiating. Check units, degree-one value scaling and degree-zero choices. At a tie report the whole correspondence and directional envelope. For smooth consumer data calculate the complete compensated matrix, not only own-price slopes; for producers retain negative net inputs when differentiating profit. Finally distinguish a proof for a full price domain from agreement at a few observations.

Reproduce the cases. Starting from the printed primitives, calculate the AM–GM equality bundles, differentiate before substituting prices, multiply each curvature matrix by its full price vector, and verify the supplied square certificates. Evaluate both the active and inactive entry plans at each boundary. Rational arithmetic suffices for every printed numerical case. The formulas establish global optima and full branches; a numerical grid alone would not establish the proofs.

Teach-back. In two minutes explain why expenditure has a negative-semidefinite price Hessian but profit has a positive-semidefinite one, why Roy’s ratio can fail with unique choice, and what every profit value fails to identify.

Illustrative teach-back answer

Expenditure minimizes fixed feasible bundles’ linear costs, so its value lies below their supporting planes and is concave. Profit maximizes fixed feasible production plans’ linear receipts, so it is convex. Their gradients, when qualified envelopes apply, are compensated consumption and net supply. A strictly increasing numerical transformation can have a zero derivative: the cubic total-goods example makes both Roy numerator and denominator zero while preserving unique demand. Finally linear profit objectives see the convex free-disposal hull, so the original entry technology and its hull share every positive-price value while differing on the plan (−4,1). Full credit requires these mechanisms and their conditions, not only the words “duality” or “convexity.”

Delayed retention. Without reopening the derivations, return after several days: (i) state why target 1 may be unattainable for u=1−exp(−Σx); (ii) recover the compensated matrix’s null price direction in case 1; (iii) decide whether increasing both input and output prices by the same positive factor changes case 5 quantities; (iv) explain why profit’s capacity boundary and entry boundary have different envelope behavior.

Retention answers and scoring

(i) Every finite bundle has utility strictly below 1, so expenditure is +∞ and Hicksian demand empty at that target. (ii) S(4,1)′=0; its quadratic form is −(d₁−4d₂)²/8. (iii) q=r/[4√(w₁w₂)] and the input-price ratios are unchanged by common scaling, so all quantities stay fixed and monetary profit scales. (iv) Entry has two distinct optimal plans and output-price slopes 0 and 2; at capacity there is one plan with matching first derivatives, although the second derivative changes. Give one point for each correct conclusion and one for its stated reason, for eight points. Rework the relevant proof after any missing reason.

Exercises

  1. Existence and target boundaries. Prove both consumer dual identities and both correspondence equalities on ℝ+L, stating the continuity, price, target and local-nonsatiation assumptions at the steps that use them. Diagnose expenditure at target 1 for u(x)=1−exp(−Σxi).
  2. Compensation and signs. On the shifted domain in case 1 derive Marshallian and Hicksian demand globally, including zero surplus. At p=(4,1),m=14 compute the full price Jacobian, income derivative and Slutsky matrix. Recompute demand after p changes to (9,1), and derive the two positive money-loss measures with their reference prices and utilities.
  3. Every minimizing bundle. For u=x₁+2x₂, target 6 and p=(2,4), derive the entire Hicksian set and the directional derivative for every direction d. Prove that each minimizer is a supporting supergradient and explain why no single ordinary gradient exists.
  4. An invalid Roy division. Prove unique demand for u=(x₁+x₂−3)³ when p₁<p₂. Find all income and price derivatives of its indirect utility at (1,2,3). Recover the unchanged demand using an ordinally equivalent index with a valid nonzero denominator.
  5. A demand-system diagnostic. Derive case 3’s share derivatives, budget identity, homogeneity and negative own-price derivatives on the stated open domain. Calculate the complete Slutsky matrix at p=(1,1,1),m=3 and prove both its quadratic-form inequality and its precise incompatibility with a regular smooth expenditure rationalization.
  6. Constructive integrability transfer. For α>0 apply the homothetic construction to cα(p)=α√(p₁p₂)+p₃. Derive an explicit direct utility index, expenditure and the full Hicksian optimum. At α=1,p=(9,1,2),target 4 give the minimizing bundle, expenditure and achieved utility. State which global hypotheses make the construction valid.
  7. Path integrals and a constant. Integrate case 4’s compensated demands at target 3 along both coordinate paths from (1,4,2) to (4,1,2), displaying the two segment contributions for each path. Assess c+1 as a proposed unit-expenditure primitive having the same gradient.
  8. Which curvature? Derive case 5’s inputs and cost at every q≥0 by a global bound and equality conditions. Prove concavity in input prices and convexity in output. With output price 8, swap input prices from (1,4) to (4,1) and calculate output, inputs, cost and profit.
  9. The full producer Hessian. Derive case 5’s profit and net supply, prove finite attained global optimality, and calculate the complete Hessian at (w₁,w₂,r)=(1,4,8). Prove positive semidefiniteness and the Euler null direction analytically, without a numerical eigenvalue guess. State the boundary qualification at r=0.
  10. Entry is a choice. Derive every entry and capacity branch of case 6, including equality boundaries and inactive supply. Calculate all outcomes at w=1 and r=3,4,5,7. Explain the failure of an FOC-only answer at r=3 and the different differentiability conclusions at entry and capacity.
  11. A reconstruction theorem and its limit. Prove that for compact nonempty K the positive-price support inequalities reconstruct co(K)−ℝ+L. Supply the compact-hull, closedness, separation and strictly-positive-normal steps. Exhibit a point missing from case 6’s original technology that all positive-price profit observations fail to distinguish.
  12. Referee memorandum, 12 points. A paper claims: “Budget balance, homogeneity and negative own-price effects establish global rationality. Every strictly monotone utility permits Roy division. Observing the entire profit function uniquely identifies even a nonconvex technology.” Assess the three claims with explicit counterexamples and corrected hypotheses. Distinguish limited observed-price agreement from a theorem on the full price domain, and identify an informative additional observation or maintained assumption for each claim. Award 4 points per claim: diagnosis, witness, corrected theorem and evidence or scope repair.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. Continuity on the compact positive-price budget gives a demanded bundle. For an attainable target ū≥u(0), choose a feasible z and minimize on the closed contour intersected with {p·x≤p·z}; this compact restriction loses no cheaper solution. If a minimizer h delivered excess utility, the continuous path th from zero would attain the target at some t<1 and lower cost. Thus u(h)=ū. Local nonsatiation makes every demanded bundle exhaust income; otherwise a small better perturbation remains affordable. The same argument excludes any cheaper bundle attaining v, proving e(p,v)=m and making exactly those expenditure minimizers the original utility maximizers.

    Conversely h attains ū at expenditure e. A bundle in B(p,e) with strictly higher utility could be radially reduced to a strictly cheaper target-achieving bundle, contradicting e. Therefore v(p,e)=ū. Every demand at e exhausts that budget under local nonsatiation and reaches the same target, and every Hicksian minimizer is a demand, giving the second correspondence equality. At m=0 or target u(0), the zero bundle handles the boundary. For u=1−exp(−Σx), every finite bundle has u<1; the target set at 1 is empty, so e=+∞ and H is empty. A limit as quantities diverge does not constitute an attained finite bundle.

  2. Write z=x−(1,2)≥0 and M=m−p₁−2p₂≥0. AM–GM bounds p₁z₁+p₂z₂ below by 2√(p₁p₂z₁z₂); for a target ū the equality conditions give h=(1+ū√(p₂/p₁),2+ū√(p₁/p₂)) and e=p₁+2p₂+2ū√(p₁p₂). Under a budget the same inequality bounds utility above by M/[2√(p₁p₂)], attained uniquely by x=(1+M/(2p₁),2+M/(2p₂)). At M=0 positive prices leave only the subsistence bundle.

    At the original prices M=8,x=(2,6),u=2. Differentiation gives Dpx=((−3/8,−1/4),(−1/2,−5)) and xm=(1/8,1/2). Adding xmx′ gives S=((−1/8,1/2),(1/2,−2)). Its square certificate is −(d₁−4d₂)²/8, so it is symmetric, negative semidefinite and has price null vector (4,1). At new prices subsistence costs 11,M=3,x′=(7/6,7/2),u′=1/2. The restoration equation at new prices is 14+CV=e((9,1),2)=23, giving positive loss CV=9. At old prices 14−EV=e((4,1),1/2)=8, giving positive loss EV=6. The reference utility and price in these two equations differ.

  3. Every feasible bundle has x₁+2x₂≥6 and expenditure 2x₁+4x₂=2(x₁+2x₂)≥12. Equality holds exactly on the nonnegative segment x₁+2x₂=6, including both endpoints (6,0),(0,3). Every member h remains feasible at any positive q, so e(q,6)≤q·h=12+(q−p)·h, its supporting-supergradient inequality. Directly e(p+td,6)=6 min(2+td₁,2+td₂/2), so the right directional derivative is min(6d₁,3d₂). With d=(1,0) it is 0, while with d=(−1,0) it is −6; no linear functional of d can have both values. Equivalently the ordinary p₁ slopes from the left and right are 6 and 0.

  4. Strictly increasing cubing preserves maximization of x₁+x₂. At p₁<p₂, any positive spending on good 2 can be shifted to good 1 to buy more total goods, and strict monotonicity exhausts the budget. The unique demand is (m/p₁,0). Write z=m/p₁−3. Then v=z³, vm=3z²/p₁, vp₁=−3mz²/p₁² and vp₂=0. At (1,2,3),z=0, so all three vanish. Roy’s undivided identity vp=−vmx remains true, but its ratio is undefined.

    The index x₁+x₂ is ordinally equivalent and has indirect value m/p₁. Its derivatives at the point are (−3,0,1) in price1,price2,income order, so −vp/vm=(3,0). This correction changes the numerical representation without changing any preference or feasible budget.

  5. On the declared log-spread domain each log difference has magnitude below 1, so si∈(1/4,5/12). Cyclic cancellation gives Σs=1. Common price scaling leaves every log difference unchanged; simultaneous income scaling therefore leaves m si/pi unchanged. The own share derivative is zero, so the own demand derivative is −m si/pi²<0. Off diagonal ∂si/∂pj=Aij/(12pj), and xim=si/pi. Combining these derivatives produces Sij=m[Aij/12+sisj−1{i=j}si]/(pipj).

    At the anchor this is the matrix printed in case 3, with diagonal −2/3 and cyclic off-diagonal entries 7/12 and 1/12. Let P=I−11′/3, so P=P′=P², and S=−P+A/4. Because A is skew, z′Az=0, giving z′Sz=−‖Pz‖²≤0; A and P also annihilate 1 on both sides. Yet S₁₂≠S₂₁. In a regular smooth expenditure model S is a Hessian with continuous mixed derivatives and must be symmetric. That necessary condition fails at an interior point, so such a rationalization on this neighborhood is impossible. Neither the quadratic inequality nor the three preliminary demand checks substitutes for symmetry, and none establishes a generic global theorem.

  6. For α>0, cα is positive, C¹, degree one and has nonnegative gradient on all strictly positive prices. Its Hessian quadratic form is −α√(p₁p₂)(d₁/p₁−d₂/p₂)²/4≤0, so it is concave. The constructed index is Uα(x)=min(2√(x₁x₂)/α,x₃). To achieve ū≥0 requires x₁x₂≥α²ū²/4 and x₃≥ū. AM–GM then gives minimum e=ū[α√(p₁p₂)+p₃], with unique equality bundle h=(αū√(p₂/p₁)/2,αū√(p₁/p₂)/2,ū), including the unique zero-target solution. The infimum construction gives this same index by the weighted-average and limiting-price argument in case 4, replacing 2√(q₁q₂) by α√(q₁q₂).

    At α=1,p=(9,1,2),ū=4 the result is ((2/3,6,4),20,4) in bundle, expenditure, achieved-utility order: the first two quantities have product 4, so 2√4=4, matching x₃. The proof uses the full-domain positive, concave, homogeneous price primitive and the explicit witness; it does not infer global integrability from finitely many sample prices.

  7. At fixed target 3, h₁=3√(p₂/p₁), h₂=3√(p₁/p₂),h₃=3. First change p₁ at p₂=4: ∫₁⁴6p₁−1/2dp₁=12. Then change p₂ from4 to1 at p₁=4: ∫₄¹6p₂−1/2dp₂=−12. Reverse the order: at p₁=1, ∫₄¹3p₂−1/2dp₂=−6; at p₂=1, ∫₁⁴3p₁−1/2dp₁=6. Each complete path has integral zero, agreeing with expenditure18 at both endpoints.

    The primitive c+1 has the same derivative, but it is not degree one: c(tp)+1=t c(p)+1 differs from t[c(p)+1]. Euler also gives p·∇(c+1)=c rather than c+1. For ū>0, the proposed Hicksian gradient costs ūc, less than the claimed minimum ū(c+1), so it cannot be the same expenditure system. Adding a constant is mathematically invisible to gradients but economically constrained by value homogeneity.

  8. The constraint f(k,l)≥q is equivalent to kl≥q⁴. Therefore w₁k+w₂l≥2√(w₁w₂kl)≥2q²√(w₁w₂). Equal weighted inputs and product equality attain the lower bound, yielding k=q²√(w₂/w₁),l=q²√(w₁/w₂). If q=0, positive prices uniquely select k=l=0. The price Hessian has the nonpositive quadratic form −q²√(w₁w₂)(d₁/w₁−d₂/w₂)²/2, whereas differentiating with respect to output gives Cqq=4√(w₁w₂)>0. No contradiction arises because the fixed variable differs.

    At w=(4,1),r=8, √(w₁w₂)=2 and the optimal q=8/(4·2)=1. Conditional inputs become k=1/2,l=2; cost4 and revenue8 give profit4. They exchange with the original inputs while output and profit stay fixed. These are global solutions from the bound and completed square, not merely stationary candidates.

  9. After conditional input minimization, profit over q≥0 is rq−2sq², s=√(w₁w₂)>0. Completing the square gives its finite maximum r²/(8s) at q=r/(4s), feasible for r≥0. Equality in the input bound then gives the unique inputs. For r>0, differentiation yields ∇π=(−π/(2w₁),−π/(2w₂),2π/r)=(−k,−l,q). At (1,4,8) this equals (−2,−1/2,1), and the price dot product equals profit4.

    The Hessian has entries π₁₁=3π/(4w₁²),π₂₂=3π/(4w₂²),π₁₂=π/(4w₁w₂),πᵢr=−π/(wᵢr),πrr=2π/r², giving exactly ((3,1/4,−1/2),(1/4,3/16,−1/8),(−1/2,−1/8,1/8)) at the anchor. For a=dw₁/w₁,b=dw₂/w₂,ρ=dr/r its quadratic form is π[2(ρ−(a+b)/2)²+(a−b)²/4], proving PSD for every direction. Common proportional scaling has a=b=ρ; direct matrix multiplication gives D²π(w₁,w₂,r)′=0. At r=0 the optimum is q=k=l=0,π=0; formulas with division by r are not to be evaluated there. The explicit π=r²/(8s) supplies any needed one-sided derivatives on the stated r≥0 domain.

  10. The active objective divided by w is aq−4−q². On [0,3] its unique maximizer is min(a/2,3). For a≤6 the active maximum is a²/4−4, which is negative below4, zero at4 and positive above4. Inactivity thus wins below4, ties the unique active q=2 at4, and loses above4. For a≥6, the active optimum is q=3 with profit3r−13w, positive throughout that range; at6 the interior and capacity quantities coincide. This gives every branch and tie.

    At w=1 and r=3,4,5,7, the complete output choices are 0,{0,2},5/2,3 and profits0,0,9/4,8. At3 the stationary q=3/2 has active profit−7/4, so the global optimum is inactivity. At entry the original supply set is {(0,0),(−8,2)} and the output-price slopes are0 and2, preventing differentiability. At capacity r=6, both formulas have gradient(−13,3) in (w,r) order, so the envelope is differentiable; the r second derivatives are1/(2w) on the interior side and0 on the capped side. First-derivative matching does not imply C² smoothness.

  11. Reduce any convex combination of more than L+1 generators by affine dependence of (k,1): shift its weights along a zero-sum dependence until one positive weight disappears, preserving the point and nonnegativity. Repetition represents every hull point with at most L+1 generators. The compact product of KL+1 and the closed simplex has that hull as a continuous image, so co(K) is compact. For a convergent sequence yn=an−bn, take a convergent subsequence of an; then bn converges to a−y≥0, proving the disposal hull closed. It is convex and free-disposal.

    Every point in this hull satisfies the support inequalities, since nonnegative prices cannot reward disposal and a convex combination cannot exceed a generator’s largest value. For a point outside, strict separation supplies a normal with finite separating support. A negative component is impossible because disposal would make support infinite. The nonzero normal is thus nonnegative. Add ε1: bounded K makes its support continuous, with change at most ε maxK|1·k|. For sufficiently small ε the original positive separation gap remains after allowing also the ε1·z term. This gives a strictly positive separating price and proves the reverse inclusion.

    Linear support of K−ℝ+L equals that of its convex hull at every positive price, so profits cannot reveal nonconvex gaps. In case6, (−4,1) is the half mixture of inactivity and (−8,2); producing one unit in the original set requires at least5 inputs, so the point is missing there. At entry the hull also adds a whole supply segment while the original supplies only its endpoints. A finite list of price observations gives weaker information still: the theorem’s intersection uses all strictly positive prices.

  12. Illustrative referee assessment. The first claim confuses preliminary demand consistency with integrability. Case3 has positive shares on its stated scale-invariant neighborhood, budget exhaustion, degree-zero demand and strictly negative own-price effects. Its compensated matrix nevertheless has S₁₂=7/12 and S₂₁=1/12, violating the symmetric Hessian required by regular smooth expenditure rationalization. Even a negative quadratic form fails to detect that skew component. A defensible replacement states the smooth necessary restrictions and their domain; a constructive global conclusion needs an actual theorem such as the specified homothetic c construction. Additional compensated cross-price evidence can test symmetry; finite agreement alone cannot establish the full-domain theorem.

    The second claim confuses ordinal monotonicity with a nonzero derivative of a chosen numerical index. The cubic total-goods example is strictly increasing in total goods and has unique demand, but vm=vp=0 at the stated point. The valid theorem requires differentiability at an interior income-price point and vm>0 before division. Replacing the utility label by total goods restores a valid ratio without any change in observed choices. More choice data cannot identify the derivative scale of an ordinal representation; the representation and differentiability restriction must be supplied.

    The third claim exceeds what a linear support function records. Case6 and its convex free-disposal hull share every positive-price profit, while only the hull permits (−4,1). A corrected reconstruction assumes the technology is already the closed convex free-disposal set generated by a compact K, and uses the full positive-price support function. Direct feasibility evidence about the disputed mixture, or a justified technological convexity assumption, could distinguish the technologies; another profit-value observation cannot distinguish these particular full-domain-equivalent models. At ties even their supply correspondences differ.

    Scoring. For each claim award 1 point for the precise error, 1 for the explicit counterexample or calculation, 1 for correctly delimited replacement hypotheses, and 1 for the evidence or scope repair, totaling12. Alternative valid counterexamples and evidence plans earn full credit. Merely writing “more assumptions are needed” does not earn the witness or repair points. No particular policy opinion is required.

Sources, limits and continuation

The consumer methods are contextualized by Alexander Wolitzky’s MIT 14.121 consumer-theory lectures, with the retained inspection covering the indicated demand, expenditure, envelope and Slutsky pages. Producer methods are contextualized by Scott Condie’s Advanced Microeconomic Theory, section 3.2. These are method sources; the cases, proof presentations, counterexamples and exercises here are original. Mutable source retrieval dates are not treated as publication dates.

This chapter proves a bounded set of duality results with explicit domains. It does not supply a general global Marshallian-integrability theorem, recover nonconvex technologies from profit values, or turn synthetic cases into empirical welfare estimates. The next chapter, Uncertainty and information, develops expected utility, risk comparisons and the value of information; the ordinal and monetary distinctions here will need to be preserved when choices concern lotteries.

Sources and further study

  • Alexander Wolitzky, MIT 14.121: Lectures 3–4, Consumer Theory (Fall 2015) — Primary course-method reference for indirect utility, budget multipliers and Roy's identity, expenditure/Hicksian demand, price concavity, Shephard's lemma, dual identities and Slutsky restrictions. Chapter independently supplies its own finite-dimensional proofs, explicit target and positive-derivative restrictions, and numerical cases. Graduate V13-C02 adds full original compact-optimizer envelope/directional proofs, regular Slutsky restrictions and a constructive homothetic duality class.
  • Scott Condie — Advanced Microeconomic Theory Class Notes, Chapter 3: The Theory of Supply, section 3.2 — Author-hosted teaching source for production sets/free disposal, supply and conditional-factor-demand correspondences, cost homogeneity/price concavity, Shephard's lemma and output convexity under concave technology. Graduate V13-C02 independently proves qualified net-supply envelopes and positive-price recovery of a compact-generated convex free-disposal hull.
